rows.question: Which company built the spacecraft Michael Collins stayed in while the first Moon landing took place?
rows.answer: Michael Collins stayed in lunar orbit aboard the command module Columbia during the landing [[michael-collins]] "[stated] Stayed in lunar orbit aboard the command module Columbia during the landing (src: NASA Apollo 11 mission page, 2026-10-24)". Columbia was part of the command and service module, which North American Aviation built [[command-service-module]] "[stated] Built by North American Aviation (src: NASA history, 2026-10-24)". North American Aviation was the prime contractor for the Apollo command and service module [[north-american-aviation]] "[stated] Prime contractor for the Apollo command and service module (src: NASA history, 2026-10-24)".

rows.question: For about how long were the heaters of the tank that later exploded on Apollo 13 run on ground power before launch, and what did the investigating board say started the explosion?
rows.answer:
Heaters ran for about eight hours. The source says the tank was emptied before launch by running its heaters on 65-volt ground power for about eight hours [[oxygen-tank-2]] "[stated] Before launch it was emptied by running its heaters on 65-volt ground power for about eight hours (src: Moonport SP-4204, 2026-10-24)".

The board traced the explosion to an electrically started fire in oxygen tank No. 2 [[apollo-13-review-board]] "[stated] Traced the explosion to an electrically started fire in oxygen tank No. 2 (src: Apollo 13 Review Board report, 2026-10-24)". The board's report calls the switch failure a serious oversight in which all parties share [[apollo-13-review-board-report]] "[stated] Called the switch failure a serious oversight in which all parties share (src: Michigan Daily 1970 coverage, 2026-10-24)".

The notes do not name the switch failure as the board's stated cause in those exact words, though the oxygen tank note says its thermostatic switches caused the explosion. That link is a summary line without a matching fact, so I have left it out.

rows.question: The landing site described in the Apollo 11 Mission Report's powered-descent section was named by an astronaut. What was first about the Gemini flight he commanded, and when was it?

returned: jim-lovell | 8.16 | description: Apollo 13 commander who had already orbited the Moon on Apollo 8
saturn-v | 5.02 | - [stated] First launched uncrewed on Apollo 4 on 1967-11-09 (src: NASA history, 2026-10-24)
apollo-11 | 4.88 | description: "July 1969 first crewed lunar landing: Armstrong, Aldrin and Collins, Eagle landed at Tranquility Base"

rows.answer:
The landing site is Tranquility Base. The Apollo 11 Mission Report's powered-descent section is the chunk whose description mentions the landing point, and Neil Armstrong named the site at touchdown ([[tranquility-base]] "[stated] Named by Neil Armstrong at touchdown: Houston, Tranquility Base here, the Eagle has landed (src: NASA Apollo 11 mission page, 2026-10-24)"). The section's description reads "Section 5.3, pages 5-4 to 5-6: five computer alarms, crater avoidance, manual control, landing point and propellant use" ([[apollo-11-mission-report-ch-05]] description). Its own fact lines do not name the site, so the link between the section and Tranquility Base rests on that description and the note's link to the site.

The Gemini flight he commanded was Gemini 8, in 1966. It was first in that it was the first docking of two spacecraft in orbit ([[neil-armstrong]] "[stated] Earlier commanded Gemini 8 in 1966, the first docking of two spacecraft in orbit (src: NASA biography, 2026-10-24)").

rows.question: The tank that crippled Apollo 13 was carried by a spacecraft. Which Apollo 11 crew member piloted that kind of spacecraft, and what did he do during the landing?
rows.answer:
The tank that crippled Apollo 13 was Oxygen tank No. 2. Its note says it exploded on 1970-04-13 ([[oxygen-tank-2]] "[stated] Exploded on 1970-04-13, about 56 hours into the flight (src: NASA Apollo 13 mission page, 2026-10-24)"). The note links it to the command and service module ("carried by [[command-service-module]]"). The command and service module's service module carried the oxygen tanks ([[command-service-module]] "[stated] Its service module carried the oxygen tanks that supplied power and air (src: NASA history, 2026-10-24)").

The Apollo 11 crew member who piloted that spacecraft was Michael Collins, the command module pilot ([[michael-collins]] "[stated] Command module pilot of Apollo 11 (src: NASA Apollo 11 mission page, 2026-10-24)"). He did not land on the Moon. During the landing he stayed in lunar orbit aboard the command module Columbia ([[michael-collins]] "[stated] Stayed in lunar orbit aboard the command module Columbia during the landing (src: NASA Apollo 11 mission page, 2026-10-24)").

rows.question: How did the Cortright report describe the switch failure?
rows.answer:
The Cortright report, the Report of the Apollo 13 Review Board, called the switch failure a serious oversight that all parties share [[apollo-13-review-board-report]] "[stated] Called the switch failure a serious oversight in which all parties share (src: Michigan Daily 1970 coverage, 2026-10-24)".

It also recommended removing all electrical equipment from inside the oxygen tank pressure vessel [[apollo-13-review-board-report]] "[stated] Recommended removing all electrical equipment from inside the oxygen tank pressure vessel (src: Michigan Daily 1970 coverage, 2026-10-24)".

The switches in question belong to oxygen tank No. 2. Their thermostatic switches were built to a 1962 specification for 28 volts DC [[oxygen-tank-2]] "[stated] Its thermostatic switches were built to a 1962 specification for 28 volts DC (src: Moonport SP-4204, 2026-10-24)". The heater specification was revised in 1965 to 65 volts, but the switches were not changed [[oxygen-tank-2]] "[stated] The heater specification was revised in 1965 to 65 volts but the switches were not changed (src: Moonport SP-4204, 2026-10-24)".

The notes do not give the report's own wording on the switch failure beyond these summaries.

rows.question: Put every 1970 date the brain records for Apollo 13 in order, with what happened on each.
rows.answer:
Here are the 1970 dates the brain records for Apollo 13, in order. The earlier citations dropped the `[stated]` tag that starts each fact line, so I've restored it.

1. **1970-04-06: Crew physicals.** Blood tests from the physicals showed Ken Mattingly had no rubella immunity. [[rubella-crew-swap]] "[stated] Blood tests from the 1970-04-06 physicals showed Ken Mattingly had no rubella immunity (src: NASA history Apollo 13 measles article, 2026-10-24)"

2. **1970-04-10: Crew swap.** The swap was decided at a KSC management meeting and announced at a press conference. Jack Swigert replaced Mattingly as command module pilot. [[rubella-crew-swap]] "[stated] The swap was decided at a KSC management meeting and announced at a press conference on 1970-04-10 (src: NASA history Apollo 13 measles article, 2026-10-24)"; [[apollo-13]] "[stated] Command module pilot is Jack Swigert (was Ken Mattingly, changed 1970-04-10 by KSC management meeting) (src: NASA history Apollo 13 measles article, 2026-10-24)"

3. **1970-04-11: Launch.** [[apollo-13]] "[stated] Launched 1970-04-11 (src: NASA Apollo 13 mission page, 2026-10-24)"

4. **1970-04-13: Oxygen tank explosion and abort.** Oxygen tank No. 2 exploded about 56 hours into the flight. The mission goal changed from a lunar landing at Fra Mauro to a safe return to Earth, by the Mission Control abort decision. [[oxygen-tank-2]] "[stated] Exploded on 1970-04-13, about 56 hours into the flight (src: NASA Apollo 13 mission page, 2026-10-24)"; [[apollo-13]] "[stated] Mission goal became a safe return to Earth (was a lunar landing at Fra Mauro, changed 1970-04-13 by Mission Control abort decision) (src: NASA Apollo 13 mission page, 2026-10-24)"

5. **1970-04-17: Splashdown.** The crew, using the lunar module Aquarius as a lifeboat, splashed down. [[apollo-13]] "[stated] Crew used the lunar module Aquarius as a lifeboat and splashed down on 1970-04-17 (src: NASA Apollo 13 mission page, 2026-10-24)"
